title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The design used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial LLM generation per task, reused across both arms) and allowed up to one validator‑triggered repair in the guarded arm. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial) using the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier. All archived scoring artifacts show every paired episode was scored safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The primary estimand is therefore empirically uninformative in this run because the single shared initial candidates passed deterministic validation for every task and no repairs were invoked. We report the preregistered design, execution accounting, artifact‑grounded analysis, an explicit mechanism explaining the null paired contrast, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Translating high‑level operator intent into safe, executable device configurations is a central NetOps objective. Large language models (LLMs) offer flexible intent‑to‑configuration generation, but textual fidelity alone does not guarantee ordering, dependency preservation, or invariant satisfaction necessary for safe network changes. Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluation—where generated configurations are applied to device images or deterministic simulators and semantically scored—exposes operational failure modes (ordering errors, transient violations, protected‑resource touches) that text‑only benchmarks miss. A recurring architectural response is the generate–validate–repair (GVR) pattern: (1) generate a candidate with an LLM; (2) deterministically validate semantic invariants; (3) apply an automated repair when violations are found. Prior work shows promise for GVR patterns in configuration and program repair domains, but open empirical questions remain about verifier benefit under distribution shift and adversarial prompts and about experimental designs that can reliably reveal paired differences between guarded and unguarded pipelines.

We preregistered a confirmatory paired experiment to measure a single estimand precisely: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 denotes a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. The execution contract enforced shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced per task and reused across both arms; the guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. Our contributions are: (1) a fully preregistered, emulation‑grounded paired evaluation of a GVR pipeline with explicit estimand mapping to archived analysis artifacts; (2) an artifact‑grounded explanation for a degenerate paired contrast observed in the run; and (3) concrete, evidence‑based recommendations for designing future informative GVR experiments.
sections.related_work: Executable, emulation‑grounded NetOps benchmarks have recently emerged to surface planning and execution faults for LLM agents rather than only measuring textual fidelity; NetConfArena is a representative example of this closed‑loop approach. Prior system and program‑repair literature documents generate–validate patterns and shows that deterministic validators can enable high repair coverage for many syntactic and constrained semantic faults, though coverage depends on verifier design and fault taxonomy. Survey and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising patterns for operational NetOps automation and safety. Work on configuration analysis (for example, the engineering evolution of deterministic network analysis tools) provides precedent for verifier design and incremental verification strategies. Our study differs from earlier work by (a) preregistering a single paired estimand and execution contract, (b) running under shared_initial_candidate semantics that explicitly control paired generator variability, and (c) archiving per‑call traces and deterministic validator outcomes to permit precise reconciliations between design and measured estimand.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the study (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and defined the primary estimand as the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline). The preregistration specified a paired design with shared_initial_candidate generation semantics: a single initial LLM generation is produced per task and reused across the paired episodes; the guarded arm may request up to one validator‑triggered repair. The analysis plan used a paired binary executor that produces a contingency table, bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples), and an exact McNemar test on discordant pairs.

Task bank, sampling, and blocking: We executed N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks blocked into topology/vendor clusters with composition: in‑distribution 60% (144 tasks), distribution‑shift 20% (48 tasks; novel topologies/vendors held‑out from the generator), and adversarial‑prompt 20% (48 tasks; adversarial prompts generated under a preregistered adversary protocol). Tasks were deterministically generated and included initial states, required command sequences, allowed touched fields, and final invariant constraints appropriate to multi‑device maintenance workflows.

Models, adapter contract, and verifier: The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini and the registered adapter enforced shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared generation per task). The guarded pipeline used a deterministic validator designed to check workflow invariants and execution semantics; if the validator failed, the guarded adapter could invoke at most one repair iteration to produce a repaired final configuration. The adapter contract makes clear that, under shared_initial_candidate semantics, paired differences can arise only when the shared initial candidate fails validation or when a validator‑triggered repair changes the final configuration.

Scoring, exclusions, and missingness: Final outcomes were scored binary: safe (no semantic safety violation if applied) or unsafe (semantic safety violation). The preregistered exclusion rules removed items flagged as possible false‑safe (validator PASS but simulator indicates unsafe) from the primary analysis and treated irrecoverable infrastructure failures according to the retry policy. The run recorded model‑call metadata for reconciliation and analysis; missingness rules and sensitivity analyses for worst‑case treatment were prespecified.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed according to the preregistered plan. Planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480; complete pairs = 240. The execution used exactly one hosted model call per task (240 model‑call events in provider accounting), consistent with the shared_initial_candidate contract. There were no infrastructure failures requiring exclusion.

Primary outcomes and contingency: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. The observed counts were: both arms safe = 240 pairs; guarded_only_safe and baseline_only_safe discordant counts = 0. Thus the paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant pairs yields p = 1.0. These values are derived directly from the archived analysis artifacts produced by the preregistered executor.

Validator activity and repair budget utilization: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied across the entire corpus; the guarded arm did not exercise the repair path because the shared initial candidates passed deterministic validation for every task. The planned sensitivity channels (treating possible false‑safe flags or infra failures as unsafe in worst‑case analyses) were unused because no such flags or failures occurred. Reconciliation checks passed: provider call accounting, complete pair counts, and analysis bookkeeping are internally consistent with the preregistered contract.

Subgroup slices: All subgroups— in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, and adversarial‑prompt subsets—exhibit the same degenerate contingency (no unsafe applies in either arm). Therefore subgroup contrasts are numerically 0 and uninformative under the operational contract used in this run.
sections.discussion:
Mechanistic explanation for the null paired contrast: Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the single initial LLM output is shared between baseline and guarded episodes; the guarded arm gains leverage only when deterministic validation fails and repair is applied. In this execution the deterministic validator accepted every shared candidate, so the guarded pipeline never invoked repair and could not produce discordant paired outcomes. This mechanistic fact—explicit in the preregistered adapter contract and corroborated by provider accounting and validator outcomes—explains the degenerate paired contingency and the observed statistical results.

Design tradeoffs and implications: Shared_initial_candidate semantics reduce model‑call budget and ensure strict pairing of generator outputs, which simplifies paired estimand interpretation when generator variability is a confound. However, as a causal intervention to measure verifier benefit, shared_initial_candidate makes the experiment dependent on generator failures occurring in the corpus. When generator outputs are high quality for the chosen tasks and adversary strength, the guarded intervention cannot manifest. To evaluate the causal effect of a verifier it is therefore necessary to (a) allow independent initial generations per arm, (b) increase adversary strength or introduce controlled generator perturbations to produce validator triggers, or (c) expand repair budgets and repair search strategies to ensure the repair mechanism can be exercised when validation fails.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded): Internal validity is shaped by the explicit generation semantics used; the archived execution demonstrates strict adherence to the shared generation contract. Construct validity depends on verifier coverage: deterministic validators encode a finite set of checks and may miss subtle semantic fault classes despite passing many canonical invariants. External validity is limited because tasks derive from a synthetic, emulation‑grounded corpus; generalization to production multi‑vendor networks and human operational procedures requires further study. Conclusion validity here is constrained by the realized baseline unsafe rate of zero: with no observed unsafe applies the paired contrast cannot detect verifier benefit under the current contract and corpus.

Recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations (artifact‑grounded): 1) If the primary goal is to estimate verifier causal effect, avoid shared_initial_candidate semantics or explicitly allow separate initial generations per arm to create opportunities for discordance. 2) Increase adversary strength or diversify adversarial protocols to produce validator triggers; fixed‑seed adversaries may be insufficient. 3) Increase repair budgets (multiple repair iterations) and instrument repair reasoning to study repair dynamics. 4) Expand verifier semantic coverage and add cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator outcomes to detect potential false‑safe behavior. The archived execution and reconciliation artifacts provide an explicit starting point for implementing these adjustments reproducibly.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a generate–validate–repair pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. The measured paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) is 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0). This null result is artifact‑grounded and mechanistically explained by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics combined with deterministic validator PASS on every shared candidate, which prevented any repair invocation. The archived preregistration, execution accounting, validator outcomes, and analysis artifacts support this conclusion and yield concrete, reproducible recommendations for future GVR studies that seek informative paired contrasts by changing generation semantics, adversary strength, or repair budgets.

disclosure_statement: Models and orchestration: Execution used the declared hosted model gpt‑5‑mini via the registered adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The guarded pipeline used the deterministic verifier deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted at most one validator‑triggered repair per task. Preregistration and autonomy: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock. limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a synthetic, emulation‑grounded corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and made verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: the deterministic verifier implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected and could produce false‑safe outcomes under different task distributions.
